rv.q: In a crowded Broadway season, this play cranks up the volume: it hits like a drum kick to the soul.
Stereophonic, one of Broadway’s most striking plays of the season, is an allegory of industry greed and artistry.
The play is a staggering achievement, and already feels like a must-see American classic.
The result is richly satisfying multitrack production.
What a brilliant piece of must-see Broadway. It's Chekhovian, babe.
By the time the play ends, its searing emotional heft creeps up and grabs you by the throat.
Stereophonic is at the Theatre.

Audiences may feel the same way after seeing this work of theatrical virtuosity, realizing that all the tiny details, wild rhythms, and clever hooks presented on stage have added up to a work that is brave, purposeful, and rich.
David Adjmi’s “Stereophonic” is the play that sparks this very desire.
This ambitious musical about a rock band recording an album in the 1970s is a triumph of theatrical storytelling that captures the creative process in all its messy, exhilarating glory.
What we get in 'Stereophonic' is nothing short of a marvel: a play that captures the messy, intoxicating process of artistic creation with an authenticity that feels almost voyeuristic.
This backstage musical about a '70s rock band making an album is a marathon of emotional and artistic intensity that rewards patient theatergoers with an experience of rare authenticity.

All is not ill: Gayle Rankin, whose voice is a big angry miracle, plays Sally Bowles, the cabaret’s down-at-the-heels star, and she scream-sings with such total conviction that she almost sells the show as her own personal nightmare.
“Stereophonic,” directed by Daniel Aukin, is undeniably transportive, and it’s a pleasure to be immersed in this creatively robust decade for a while.
But that doesn’t even begin to describe the genius on display at the Golden Theatre.
Then again, everything about Stereophonic is remarkable from top to bottom.
Stereophonic is an absolute triumph of a show, a delicious four-course meal about a band packin' up, shackin' up, and attempting to keep their success going, as scary as it may seem.
It's a riveting, painful, funny, intense, toe-tapping journey, and the end result can best be described as solid gold.
You’ll want to live in this play forever.
Once you ease into its singular, almost fly-on-the-wall dramatic world, you’re mesmerized.
Discord gives way to perfect harmony, in an instant; it’s one of numerous times in this story — whether real or imagined — we’re reminded of the transcendent power of art, for the artists and for us.
The naturalistic, overlapping dialogue ranges from slow meditations on donuts to fiery, violent spats between bandmates, and it’s completely absorbing.
Adjmi captures that claustrophobia and inability to communicate, making his “Stereophonic” one of the very best plays to open last year Off Broadway and now this season on Broadway.
Many of the reviews have been ecstatic, some calling it a “masterpiece,” but for me, the play, for all its expertise, is too much of the same old same old.
What makes Stereophonic remarkable is its realism; capturing the deeply unglamorous moments that contribute to creative brilliance and personal disaster.

Taken as a whole, this is easily one of my favorite theatre experiences of the year, partially because the lives of audio technicians and sound designers and recording artists are not often addressed except as side characters in a world to which we are integral.

It’s hard to fault the seamless way that his carefully constructed script explores how an artistic triumph can emerge from a toxic mix of talent, interpersonal drama, easy access to drugs and alcohol, and the quest for fame.
Unfortunately the action is diluted by Daniel Aukin ’s slow direction (he could cut an hour off without changing the plot) and the levity of the script by David Adjmi.

cn.t: Critics hail Adjmi's three-hour studio drama as a masterful, immersive triumph that captures the messy creative process with stunning authenticity. The hyperrealistic production, original songs, and design dazzle, though the lengthy runtime tests some.

vs.sum: The John Golden Theatre offers good sightlines from most seats, though sound quality can vary, especially under the mezzanine. Seating comfort is typical of older theaters with tight legroom, but the venue maintains a pleasant ambiance overall. Facilities are adequate, though not exceptional.

acc.note: 5 wheelchair spaces in Orchestra. No wheelchair-accessible restroom (use adjacent Schoenfeld).

vr.q: Yes, it is 3 hours and 15 minutes, but it is some of my favorite hours that I have spent in a theater.
